newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: First defence eyewitness testifies at UN trial.
newsitem.headline: First defence eyewitness testifies at UN trial.

text.p: The first defence eyewitness in the war crimes trial of Bosnian Serb Dusan Tadic told a U.N. tribunal on Tuesday that Tadic was a defender of peoples' rights who had wanted to rebuild a shell-shattered town.
Identified only as "Witness U" for his own protection, the Bosnian Croat said from behind a screen that he knew nothing of allegations that Tadic had been a commander at a Serb-run detention camp.
Tadic, a 40-year old former cafe owner, denies charges of murdering, torturing and raping Moslems at camps in Bosnia during a Serb campaign of ethnic cleansing in 1992.

On the first day of the trial after its suspension because of Saturday's Bosnian elections, Witness U told the U.N. tribunal for former Yugoslavia about events surrounding the Serb shelling of the predominantly Moslem town of Kozarac, in northwest Bosnia, in May 1992.
The witness, a postal worker in Kozarac and married to a Serb, said he fled the town on May 27 in a column of about 3,000 Moslems, Croats and Serbs four days after the shelling began.
He returned towards the end of September to find houses destroyed and attended a residents' meeting, at which Tadic was elected secretary of the local council.
"It was because he was the greatest supporter of bringing Kozarac back to life," the witness said, adding that Tadic had told him of his hopes to rebuild the town.
Asked by counsel for the defence if Tadic's appointment had anything to do with politics, he replied: "No, it was the people who elected him because he championed the return to Kozarac."

When asked what he thought of allegations that Tadic had been a commander at Trnopolie, one of the camps in the region, he said: "I neither know anything about that nor have I heard anything like that."
Under cross-examination from prosecutor Michael Keegan, Witness U said most of the local people who had returned to Korarac and were present at the meeting were Serbs.
He said he did not know what had happened to the Moslems who had left at the same time as him at the end of May.
The prosecution alleged that before the war the witness had used his position as a postman to find out when local people received their pensions and then to ask them for money.

"You saw the war, or being on the right side of the war, as an opportunity to cancel your debts," Keegan said, adding that Witness U he had also looted his neighbours' property on returning to Kozarac.
The witness denied both allegations.
Witness U was due to be the third on the defence counsel's list but defence laywer Steven Kay told journalists the first two had withdrawn, giving no explanation.
He said the defence would next call two protected witnesses which would mean the court going into a fully closed session, probably until Friday.
Earlier on Tuesday, the court rejected a plea from Tadic's defence to have the bulk of the charges against him dropped.
In a short statement, Presiding Judge Gabrielle Kirk McDonald said the motion was denied and the trial would proceed as planned.
The trial has heard from 75 prosecution witnesses since early May.

The only other defence witness to testify so far, Robert McBeth Hayden, a professor of anthropology at the University of Pittsburgh, detailed the rising tide of nationalism in the former Yugoslavia which culminated in war.
Tadic is one of seven war crimes suspects in custody at the tribunal, which has so far indicted 75 suspects -- 54 Serbs, 18 Croats and three Moslems.
